Henceforth
hens-FORTH
adverb
From hence (“from here, from this”) + forth (“forward”); hence “from this time forward, from now on.” It looks not backward but ahead, marking a line after which all is changed.

Biblical Definition

Henceforth means from this time forward — from now on. It is a word that draws a line across a life or a history and declares that after it nothing shall be as before. The modern reader is in little danger of reversing it, but great danger of skimming it, for on that little line hang some of the weightiest turns in Scripture. At the last supper the Lord sets the line at His death: “I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine, until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom” (Mat 26:29). Paul sets it at the cross for our knowledge of Christ: “Wherefore henceforth know we no man after the flesh” (2Co 5:16) — the old carnal reckoning ends, and a new estimate of every man begins. The Lord sets it at His own self-revealing: “from henceforth ye know him, and have seen him” (Joh 14:7) — the Father made visible in the Son from that hour on. And Paul sets it at our union with the crucified Christ: our old man is crucified with Him, “that henceforth we should not serve sin” (Rom 6:6). Mark that last well. Henceforth is the grammar of the new birth. There is a decisive before and after in the Christian’s life, and the believer lives on the far side of a line grace has drawn. What he was, he is no more; henceforth he is Christ’s.

Webster 1828 Definition

From this time forward; from now on; from this point onward.

HENCEFORTH, from this time forward; onward from the present.

From hence (“from this”) + forth (“forward”).

It looks ahead, marking a line after which all is changed.

Christ would drink no more of the vine henceforth, until the kingdom (Mat 26:29).

Crucified with Christ, henceforth we should not serve sin (Rom 6:6).

Key Scripture

Mat 26:29 — "But I say unto you, I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine, until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom."

2Co 5:16 — "Wherefore henceforth know we no man after the flesh: yea, though we have known Christ after the flesh, yet now henceforth know we him no more."

Joh 14:7 — "If ye had known me, ye should have known my Father also: and from henceforth ye know him, and have seen him."

Rom 6:6 — "Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin."

Modern Corruption

A plain word for “from now on”; it recovers the decisive line grace draws between the old life and the new.

expand to see more

There is no corruption of sense to fight here, only the reader’s temptation to hurry past a small word that carries a large weight. “Henceforth” announces a dividing line: a before and an after, a point past which the terms of life are altered. When the Lord says He will drink no more of the vine henceforth until the kingdom, He is marking the eve of His death as a boundary. When Paul says henceforth we know no man after the flesh, he is dating a whole new way of seeing from the cross. Skim the word and the boundary vanishes.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the decisive character of conversion. The gospel is not a gradual improvement of the old man but his crucifixion and the raising of a new: our old man is crucified with Christ, that henceforth we should not serve sin. There is a real line in the believer’s history — not always felt in a single moment, but true in fact — before which he was under sin’s dominion and after which he is not. This is the ground of all pursuit of holiness: not “become what you are not” by mere effort, but “be what you now are” in Christ. Reckon ye yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin. Henceforth is the word of a redeemed man, and it faces forward.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means from this time forward, from now on — a line after which all is changed.

"“Henceforth know we no man after the flesh” — the old reckoning ends at the cross."
